items.explanation: Bare "little" stresses how limited the experience is. "A little" stresses the existence of some experience, which would support a more positive argument.

This highlights the experience the group does have. It does not preserve the requested emphasis on near-absence.
Bare little gives the negative orientation needed to explain the cancellation.
rationales.We have a little of the experience of cl: This awkwardly treats the experience as an identified whole with a small portion; that is not the general lack described.
rationales.We have the little experience of climbin: "The little experience" normally needs a defining continuation such as "we gained last year". It does not express the intended general shortfall here.

findings: Original clearer-policy item used formal content for an elementary a decision.
audit.microSkill: Bare little versus a little in an explanatory argument
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how article choice affects whether a quantity supports or undermines a conclusion.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting the reason for a decision through quantity orientation suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: A negative uncountable evaluation, distinct from the positive invitation with seats.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the first phrase.
items.taskText: A website adds an unexpected fee at the final payment step. Its designer calls this 'confusing by design'. What does 'by design' mean?
options: Confusing because the design has not yet been completed
Deliberately confusing as a planned part of the payment process
Confusing despite a plan intended to make the process clear
Confusing in its layout rather than in the information it presents
items.answer: Deliberately confusing as a planned part of the payment process
items.explanation: By design is an article-free expression meaning intentionally. It says the confusing effect was planned, not that the design was unfinished or that only the visual layout causes difficulty.

rationales.Confusing because the design has not yet: The fixed phrase states intention. It does not attribute the confusion to unfinished work.
rationales.Deliberately confusing as a planned part: By design presents the confusing effect as deliberate, even though the phrase contains no article before design.
rationales.Confusing despite a plan intended to mak: Despite the plan would describe an unintended result. By design says the result was intended.
rationales.Confusing in its layout rather than in t: Design here is part of an idiom about intention; it does not limit the problem to visual layout.

findings: Privacy item tested general mass reference without a substantial B2 distinction.
audit.microSkill: Zero article in the idiomatic phrase by design
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a fixed article-free phrase in a meaningful contrast.
audit.levelReason: The learner must distinguish an idiomatic abstract use from ordinary noun reference.
audit.similarityNote: Only phrase expressing intentionality.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the definite noun phrase.
items.taskText: "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
options: One electric vehicle being used as the main example throughout the paragraph
Electric cars as a technological category, rather than a particular physical vehicle
The city's first electric vehicle, treated as the beginning of a wider trend
The electric vehicles in one identified fleet, rather than the vehicle type generally
items.answer: Electric cars as a technological category, rather than a particular physical vehicle
items.explanation: A definite singular can represent a class or invention. In this general discussion, "the electric car" means the technology or vehicle type, not one physical car.

rationales.One electric vehicle being used as the m: An individual-car reading would need an identifiable vehicle. The statement about transport trends instead presents the vehicle type as an influence on cities.
rationales.Electric cars as a technological categor: The definite singular can stand for a class or technological development in a general statement.
rationales.The city's first electric vehicle, treat: The article does not give the car a first-in-history meaning; that would need wording such as the first electric car.
rationales.The electric vehicles in one identified: No fleet is identified. The category reading fits the broad claim about how cities plan their networks.

findings: Original option-that sentence was only an-before-vowel despite a following clause.
audit.microSkill: Generic definite singular for a technological category
audit.pedagogicalValue: Counters the rule that the always points to one previously mentioned object.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a category-level statement in a public-policy context suits B2 reading.
audit.similarityNote: Generic invention reference rather than an individual service or named place.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article change.
items.taskText: Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
options: It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
It says her practical knowledge is greater than that of other nurses
It identifies an event that the listener has already heard about
It says the event was unusual or dangerous
items.answer: It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
items.explanation: Uncountable "experience" can mean accumulated knowledge. "An experience" counts one event someone went through. The article itself does not tell us whether that event was unusual, dangerous, or already known.

rationales.It presents one event she lived through: This captures the change from practical knowledge to a countable episode.
rationales.It says her practical knowledge is great: The article changes the noun's sense; it does not compare anyone's expertise.
rationales.It identifies an event that the listener: The indefinite article does not itself mark a previously identified event.
rationales.It says the event was unusual or dangero: Those qualities would need additional wording; they do not follow from "an".

findings: Original review-of-policy item repeated elementary singular a.
audit.microSkill: Experience as knowledge versus an experience as an event
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents article errors caused by transferring one noun sense to another.
audit.levelReason: A familiar professional noun has a meaning contrast relevant to B2 narration.
audit.similarityNote: Knowledge-to-event change distinct from other abstract-noun examples.

items.setupText: A coordinator wants to say that every remaining volunteer stayed, not just an unspecified further group.
items.taskText: 'Four volunteers left at six. ___ stayed to finish packing.' Which phrase makes the intended reference explicit?
options: Other volunteers
Some other volunteers
The other volunteers
A few other volunteers
items.answer: The other volunteers
items.explanation: The other volunteers identifies the remainder of the relevant volunteer group after the four who left are excluded. Bare other volunteers introduces further volunteers without explicitly presenting that complete remainder.

rationales.Other volunteers: This says that further volunteers stayed. It does not explicitly identify them as the full remainder of the group.
rationales.Some other volunteers: Some presents an unspecified portion or number. It leaves open whether additional volunteers also left.
rationales.The other volunteers: The definite plural picks out the remaining members of the already established group.
rationales.A few other volunteers: A few adds a small-number claim and does not express that every remaining member stayed.

findings: The first replacement reused B1's one/the other two-member frame with abstract nouns and elementary form distractors.
audit.microSkill: Definite plural remainder versus an unspecified additional group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how the changes the scope of other in a practical account of group participation.
audit.levelReason: B2 learners must preserve the difference between an entire remainder and an unspecified subset in connected prose.
audit.similarityNote: Plural-group scope replaces the duplicated singular pair-of-objects frame.

items.setupText: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the force of the article-free expression.
items.taskText: An old resident says, 'The village has changed beyond recognition.'
options: The village has changed in ways that few people have officially acknowledged.
The village is so different that its former appearance is hard to recognise.
The village has changed, though its old appearance remains easy to recognise.
The village has become better known because people have praised its improvements.
items.answer: The village is so different that its former appearance is hard to recognise.
items.explanation: Beyond recognition means changed so much that the former appearance is hard to recognise. Recognition has no article in this fixed expression; it concerns recognising the place, not acknowledging or praising the changes.

rationales.The village has changed in ways that few: This uses recognition in the sense of acknowledgment. The resident is describing how different the village looks, not whether officials acknowledge the changes.
rationales.The village is so different that its for: The paraphrase keeps the strong degree of change expressed by beyond recognition.
rationales.The village has changed, though its old: Easy to recognise weakens and reverses the idiom's central point: the changes have made recognition difficult.
rationales.The village has become better known beca: This treats recognition as public appreciation. The phrase does not say the changes brought fame or were improvements.

findings: Original advice-versus-requirement item was elementary uncountability at B2.
audit.microSkill: Zero article in beyond recognition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Builds control of a common abstract phrase through its context-dependent sense.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting figurative change and distinguishing abstract noun senses suit B2.
audit.similarityNote: An idiom of extent, unlike the intentionality phrase by design.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence that refers to the people, not their language.
items.taskText: A travel writer is describing the inhabitants of France as a national group. Which sentence has that reading?
options: French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
A French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French have influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
items.answer: The French have influenced the neighbouring regions.
items.explanation: "The French" can name the French people collectively and takes plural agreement. Article-free "French" commonly names the language and takes singular agreement.

rationales.French has influenced the neighbouring r: This naturally names the language, while the task specifies the people.
rationales.A French has influenced the neighbouring: To refer to one person, use a countable person noun such as "a French person".
rationales.The French have influenced the neighbour: The definite group expression and plural verb identify the people collectively.
rationales.The French has influenced the neighbouri: For the national group of people, "the French" takes plural agreement, so use "have".

findings: Online-system item again tested an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: The plus nationality adjective for a collective group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Links the article to both reference and subject-verb agreement.
audit.levelReason: This noun-like adjective construction and its language/person contrast are appropriate B2 grammar.
audit.similarityNote: A national group, unlike a technological generic singular.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation that fits the purpose of each visit.
items.taskText: "During her sentence she was in prison. Years later she returned to the prison to give a talk." What does the added article help signal?
options: It contrasts imprisonment with a later visit to an identified institution.
It introduces an unfamiliar prison, then identifies a different one for the talk.
It contrasts time spent in prison generally with a return to prisoner status.
It describes her earlier circumstances, then leaves the later destination unspecified.
items.answer: It contrasts imprisonment with a later visit to an identified institution.
items.explanation: "In prison" conventionally describes imprisonment. "The prison" identifies a particular institution; the talk establishes that the later visit is not another statement of prisoner status.

rationales.It contrasts imprisonment with a later v: Bare in prison expresses prisoner status; the definite phrase identifies the institution she later visits for a talk.
rationales.It introduces an unfamiliar prison, then: The first phrase expresses imprisonment rather than introducing an unfamiliar institution with a. The wording does not establish a change of prison.
rationales.It contrasts time spent in prison genera: The later purpose is giving a talk. The prison identifies her destination without saying that she is imprisoned again.
rationales.It describes her earlier circumstances,: The later definite article presents the destination as identifiable, not unspecified.

findings: Original only-entrance sentence forced a basic definite article.
audit.microSkill: Bare institutional status versus definite institutional reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how article choice works with a stated purpose, rather than merely naming a building.
audit.levelReason: Tracking a change in social role across a narrative is suitable B2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: A status-to-visit contrast rather than schooling or legal-proceeding examples.

items.setupText: A charity tested a new service in one town before expanding it. Choose the interpretation of the indefinite noun phrase.
items.taskText: "The pilot was a success, although the wider programme still faced difficulties." What does "a success" mean?
options: Success as an abstract quality of every part of the programme
One undertaking judged to have achieved a good result
The only successful activity in the organisation's history
A successful person appointed to manage the programme
items.answer: One undertaking judged to have achieved a good result
items.explanation: "A success" classifies the pilot as a successful undertaking. It is a countable result use, whereas article-free "success" can name the abstract idea.

rationales.Success as an abstract quality of every: The article makes the pilot a countable example of success; the following clause explicitly limits the wider conclusion.
rationales.One undertaking judged to have achieved: This captures the predicative countable use in "was a success".
rationales.The only successful activity in the orga: The indefinite article classifies one case; it does not make an only-ever claim.
rationales.A successful person appointed to manage: The subject is the pilot undertaking, not a person.

findings: Original pilot-study item only tested a before a consonant.
audit.microSkill: A success as a countable evaluative classification
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a useful way to evaluate one event without generalising to a whole programme.
audit.levelReason: The count/mass distinction and limitation of an evaluation suit B2 discourse.
audit.similarityNote: Evaluating an undertaking rather than describing an experience.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation of the two article patterns.
items.taskText: "We need evidence before deciding. The evidence from yesterday's inspection is particularly relevant." Why can the second sentence use "the"?
options: Evidence becomes a singular count noun because it comes from one inspection
The source phrase identifies a particular body of evidence
Repeating evidence requires the even if the second sentence concerns a different source
The article presents the inspection findings as conclusive rather than merely relevant
items.answer: The source phrase identifies a particular body of evidence
items.explanation: The first sentence requests evidence without identifying a body of it. The second points to evidence from a specified inspection. An uncountable noun can take "the" when its reference is identifiable.

rationales.Evidence becomes a singular count noun b: Evidence remains uncountable. One identifiable source does not turn it into a count noun.
rationales.The source phrase identifies a particula: The inspection makes this evidence identifiable; an uncountable noun can take the for that purpose.
rationales.Repeating evidence requires the even if: Word repetition alone does not require the. Here the source phrase identifies which evidence the writer means.
rationales.The article presents the inspection find: Definiteness identifies the evidence; it does not increase its strength. The sentence describes it as particularly relevant, not conclusive.

findings: Original cloze did not explain identified uncountable reference.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference to a specified body of uncountable evidence
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a noun's article choice from whether it can be counted.
audit.levelReason: Following general-to-specific reference in a decision-making context suits B2.
audit.similarityNote: A body of supporting material, distinct from an individual outcome or experience.

items.setupText: Choose the policy wording that covers travel costs as a general category, not a named journey or a fixed allowance.
items.taskText: Meals are excluded. Which sentence states the intended reimbursement policy?
options: The company reimburses travel, but not meals.
The company reimburses the journey described above, but not meals.
The company pays a travel allowance, but not a meal allowance.
The company reimburses a return journey, but not meals.
items.answer: The company reimburses travel, but not meals.
items.explanation: Bare travel names the general expense category, parallel to bare plural meals. A journey counts a trip; the journey identifies one; a travel allowance names a payment arrangement rather than reimbursement of travel costs generally.

rationales.The company reimburses travel, but not m: The two article-free nouns name categories of expenses, preserving the intended general policy.
rationales.The company reimburses the journey descr: The definite phrase limits reimbursement to an identified journey rather than the general category.
rationales.The company pays a travel allowance, but: The articles introduce countable allowances. An allowance can be a fixed payment and does not state the intended reimbursement policy.
rationales.The company reimburses a return journey,: This counts one return trip and narrows the kind of journey, neither of which is part of the intended general wording.

findings: Original public-transport blank allowed an identified-system reading.
audit.microSkill: Editing bare expense categories versus identified journeys and countable allowances
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how noun heads and article choices affect the scope of a practical policy.
audit.levelReason: Requires selecting among grammatical policy statements that differ in reference and what is being reimbursed.
audit.similarityNote: A policy-writing decision, distinct from interpreting an artist's name or an abstract quality.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation that preserves the contrast.
items.taskText: "An essay can explore a question without answering it; the essay you submitted does neither." How do the articles guide the reader?
options: A general possibility for essays is contrasted with an assessment of one identifiable submission
Both phrases refer to the submitted text, first as new information and then as known information
The first identifies a model essay already written; the second identifies a student's response to it
The first introduces an unidentified text that the writer later discovers to be the submitted essay
items.answer: A general possibility for essays is contrasted with an assessment of one identifiable submission
items.explanation: "An essay" supports a general claim through a representative example. "The essay you submitted" then singles out an identifiable text for criticism.

rationales.A general possibility for essays is cont: An essay represents a class member in the general statement; the essay you submitted then identifies the particular work being assessed.
rationales.Both phrases refer to the submitted text: The first clause describes what essays can do in general. It does not introduce the submitted essay as a particular new referent.
rationales.The first identifies a model essay alrea: No existing model or response to a model is introduced. The first noun phrase supports a general possibility.
rationales.The first introduces an unidentified tex: The passage moves from generalisation to assessment, not from ignorance to discovery of a text's identity.

findings: Original essay-at-the-end item was elementary an selection.
audit.microSkill: Generic indefinite followed by a definite individual application
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how articles structure movement from principle to case.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a generalisation and its particular application suits B2 academic feedback.
audit.similarityNote: A rhetorical general-to-specific transition rather than evidence-source identification.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite phrase.
items.taskText: "There is a reason for the delay, but I cannot discuss it yet." What does "a reason" establish?
options: The speaker presents an explanation as existing without identifying it to the listener
The speaker says the listener already knows the explanation
The speaker guarantees that only one contributing factor exists
The speaker says the delay has no explanation that could be expressed
items.answer: The speaker presents an explanation as existing without identifying it to the listener
items.explanation: The indefinite article introduces a reason while withholding its identity. It does not mean the speaker is ignorant of it, nor does it prove there is only one contributing factor.

rationales.The speaker presents an explanation as e: This separates introducing a referent from revealing which one it is.
rationales.The speaker says the listener already kn: The phrase does not mark the reason as already identifiable to the listener.
rationales.The speaker guarantees that only one con: "A reason" introduces one reason; it does not exclude further reasons.
rationales.The speaker says the delay has no explan: The opening explicitly asserts that a reason exists. The speaker is declining to discuss it.

findings: Original reason-for-rejecting cloze did not teach what indefinite reference implies.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite introduction despite speaker knowledge
audit.pedagogicalValue: Corrects the idea that a necessarily means unknown to the speaker.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting withheld information and reference status fits B2 communication.
audit.similarityNote: A reason known but withheld, rather than a hypothetical or generic referent.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that identifies the previously stated reason.
items.taskText: The memo cancels the concert because the venue is unsafe. We can dispute ___ without denying that repairs are needed.
options: a further reason given in the memo
the reason given in the memo
some other reasons given in the memo
another reason given in the memo
items.answer: the reason given in the memo
items.explanation: The earlier sentence has supplied the reason being discussed: the venue is unsafe. "The reason given in the memo" points back to that identified reason.

rationales.a further reason given in the memo: Further adds another reason instead of pointing back to the safety reason just stated.
rationales.the reason given in the memo: The definite phrase identifies the safety justification already supplied for cancelling the concert.
rationales.some other reasons given in the memo: This introduces several different reasons; the prompt asks for the one already stated.
rationales.another reason given in the memo: Another shifts to a different reason instead of maintaining reference to the safety justification.

findings: Original reason-given sentence did not establish the reason in context.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference to a reason expressed as a whole proposition
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that a prior idea can establish reference without repeating the same noun.
audit.levelReason: Following a proposal and a qualified objection is appropriate B2 discourse.
audit.similarityNote: Propositional antecedent, unlike a noun introduced in an earlier sentence.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
items.taskText: "After the interview, she felt a confidence she had never felt before." Why is "a confidence" possible?
options: It presents a particular kind or instance of the feeling, described by the following clause
It counts one secret she has told the interviewer
It identifies the feeling as already shared by all the interviewers
It means the noun confidence is always countable after felt
items.answer: It presents a particular kind or instance of the feeling, described by the following clause
items.explanation: An abstract feeling can be presented as a particular manifestation when it is characterised: "a confidence she had never felt before". This does not make every use of confidence countable.

rationales.It presents a particular kind or instanc: The following clause characterises the distinctive confidence she experienced.
rationales.It counts one secret she has told the in: "A confidence" can mean a secret in other contexts, but "felt" and the repeated feeling point to self-assurance.
rationales.It identifies the feeling as already sha: The sentence concerns her feeling and does not establish a shared state among interviewers.
rationales.It means the noun confidence is always c: Compare "She felt confidence in the plan". Countability depends on the chosen interpretation, not a universal rule after felt.

findings: Original experience-versus-certificates item allowed more than one article reading.
audit.microSkill: A characterised manifestation of an abstract feeling
audit.pedagogicalValue: Introduces a controlled exception to the no-a-with-abstract-nouns shortcut.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a described emotional state in a short narrative suits upper-intermediate reading.
audit.similarityNote: An emotional manifestation differs from practical experience as an event.

items.setupText: Choose the explanation of the definite reference.
items.taskText: "The dentist offered an appointment on Friday. Unfortunately, the time clashes with my shift." How does the listener identify "the time"?
options: As the time associated with the offered appointment
As every available appointment time on Friday
As the current clock time during the conversation
As a new unspecified time that the dentist has not offered
items.answer: As the time associated with the offered appointment
items.explanation: An appointment conventionally has a scheduled time. The offered appointment therefore makes "the time" identifiable without a previous literal mention of the word time.

rationales.As the time associated with the offered: The relationship between an appointment and its time supplies the reference.
rationales.As every available appointment time on F: The singular phrase refers to the offered appointment's time, not all available slots.
rationales.As the current clock time during the con: The clash is with a shift at the appointment time, not with the moment of speaking.
rationales.As a new unspecified time that the denti: The definite phrase depends on the appointment just offered; it does not introduce an unrelated time.

findings: Original appointment-slot item tested only a vowel-initial noun.
audit.microSkill: Associated definite reference to an appointment's time
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends reference tracking beyond repeating the same word.
audit.levelReason: The learner resolves an implied relation in a practical scheduling exchange.
audit.similarityNote: A scheduled event's attribute, unlike the physical part-whole roof example at B1.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct sentence for this meaning.
items.taskText: The speaker means people who are out of work as a group. Which sentence expresses that?
options: The unemployed need access to affordable training.
An unemployed needs access to affordable training.
The unemployeds need access to affordable training.
An unemployed people need access to affordable training.
items.answer: The unemployed need access to affordable training.
items.explanation: "The unemployed" uses the adjective to refer collectively to unemployed people. It takes plural agreement but does not add a plural -s to the adjective.

rationales.The unemployed need access to affordable: The definite article plus adjective names the group, with the plural verb "need".
rationales.An unemployed needs access to affordable: To count one person, say "an unemployed person"; unemployed does not normally stand as that singular count noun.
rationales.The unemployeds need access to affordabl: Do not add plural -s to the adjective in this group construction.
rationales.An unemployed people need access to affo: The singular article "an" cannot introduce plural "people".

findings: Original link-between-practice-and-speed item was a basic a cloze.
audit.microSkill: The plus adjective forming a collective human group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Links article choice with the limits of adjective-to-noun conversion.
audit.levelReason: This collective construction belongs in upper-intermediate discussion of social issues.
audit.similarityNote: A social category rather than the nationality example.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the repeated noun.
items.taskText: "The campaign gave the issue publicity, though not the publicity the organisers wanted." What does the second phrase do?
options: It counts one advertisement purchased by the organisers
It identifies a desired kind of public attention and contrasts it with the attention received
It states that the campaign received no public attention
It establishes that all publicity was arranged in advance
items.answer: It identifies a desired kind of public attention and contrasts it with the attention received
items.explanation: The first article-free use names public attention generally. "The publicity the organisers wanted" then identifies the particular kind or character of attention they had hoped for.

rationales.It counts one advertisement purchased by: "Publicity" remains uncountable; the sentence does not identify a purchased advertisement.
rationales.It identifies a desired kind of public a: This preserves both the existence of publicity and the qualification about its character.
rationales.It states that the campaign received no: The first clause explicitly says the issue received publicity.
rationales.It establishes that all publicity was ar: Wanting a kind of attention does not mean the actual attention was planned or controlled.

findings: Original only-link item repeated a forced definite frame.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference to a desired kind of an uncountable phenomenon
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how an identifying clause narrows an abstract noun without making it countable.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a qualified assessment of an outcome is suitable B2 reading.
audit.similarityNote: Desired versus actual publicity, distinct from identified evidence or accumulated expertise.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the two noun phrases.
items.taskText: "She studies public policy, but the policy she criticised yesterday was her own department's." How do the articles distinguish the references?
options: A field of study is contrasted with a particular departmental course of action
One established policy is contrasted with a new example of the same policy
Two particular policies are contrasted, with identifying details omitted from the first
Two fields of study are contrasted, with the second limited to work in one department
items.answer: A field of study is contrasted with a particular departmental course of action
items.explanation: Article-free "public policy" names a field. "The policy she criticised" identifies one policy through the following clause. Neither article alone tells us whether the policy has legal force or an international scope.

rationales.A field of study is contrasted with a pa: Bare public policy names the academic field. The policy she criticised identifies one adopted policy through the following clause.
rationales.One established policy is contrasted wit: The first phrase names a field rather than one established policy. The second is definite, not an indefinite introduction of a new example.
rationales.Two particular policies are contrasted,: Studying public policy describes her subject area; it does not establish a first individual policy whose details have been withheld.
rationales.Two fields of study are contrasted, with: The second phrase identifies a policy belonging to a department, not another academic discipline.

findings: Original public-policy cloze tested only a basic field-name rule.
audit.microSkill: Field reference versus a definite individual policy
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects the same noun's article pattern with two different referential roles.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting an academic field and a qualified institutional claim suits C1 precision.
audit.similarityNote: A field-to-policy shift rather than a mere contrast of identified examples.

items.setupText: Choose the reading supported by the article and modifier.
items.taskText: "The very wealthy were largely insulated from the rise in rents." What does "the very wealthy" denote?
options: A single exceptionally wealthy household already mentioned
A collective group defined by a high degree of wealth
Wealth itself considered as an abstract resource
Every person whose income rose during the period
items.answer: A collective group defined by a high degree of wealth
items.explanation: "The" allows the modified adjective phrase "very wealthy" to refer collectively to people. It takes plural agreement without turning wealthy into a plural noun.

rationales.A single exceptionally wealthy household: The adjective phrase refers collectively to wealthy people; it does not name or identify one particular household.
rationales.A collective group defined by a high deg: The definite article combines with the degree-modified adjective to identify the group.
rationales.Wealth itself considered as an abstract: The phrase refers to people who possess wealth; the abstract noun would be wealth.
rationales.Every person whose income rose during th: An increase in income does not establish that a person is very wealthy. The adjective describes a level of wealth, not a recent change.

findings: Original most-serious-limitation item was a simple superlative cloze.
audit.microSkill: The with a degree-modified adjective denoting a human group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how internal adjective modification works in a collective reference phrase.
audit.levelReason: The learner interprets an expanded collective adjective construction in analytical prose.
audit.similarityNote: Degree-defined social group, distinct from institutional roles and proper names.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
items.taskText: The proposal attracted ___ than its authors had anticipated.
options: a good many more objections
good a many more objections
a good much more objections
a good many more objection
items.answer: a good many more objections
items.explanation: "A good many" means quite a large number and takes a plural count noun. Here it modifies the comparison: "a good many more objections".

rationales.a good many more objections: The fixed quantity phrase keeps a before good many and agrees with plural objections.
rationales.good a many more objections: The order of the expression is "a good many", not "good a many".
rationales.a good much more objections: "Objections" is countable and plural; the phrase uses many rather than much.
rationales.a good many more objection: The meaning involves a number of objections, so the noun must be plural.

findings: Original unusually-cautious-interpretation item tested only a vowel sound.
audit.microSkill: Article placement in a good many with a comparative quantity
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches an idiomatic quantity phrase as part of a longer comparison.
audit.levelReason: The expanded quantifying construction is useful in C1 formal argument and commentary.
audit.similarityNote: Only fixed a good many expression.

items.setupText: Choose the inference supported by the article-free expression.
items.taskText: "The board approved the merger in principle, subject to agreement on the financing." What does "in principle" contribute?
options: Support for the merger's general idea, with financing still an outstanding condition
Support for a broad objective but opposition to this particular proposed merger
Approval of the merger without further conditions, apart from routine financial paperwork
Permission to implement the merger immediately while financing is negotiated afterwards
items.answer: Support for the merger's general idea, with financing still an outstanding condition
items.explanation: "In principle" signals assent at the level of the general idea. The financing condition shows that this is not yet unconditional approval of all practical details.

rationales.Support for the merger's general idea, w: In principle grants conceptual approval, while subject to keeps agreement on financing as a condition.
rationales.Support for a broad objective but opposi: The board expresses qualified approval of the merger itself. It does not oppose this proposal while endorsing a different broad objective.
rationales.Approval of the merger without further c: The financing qualification is an unresolved agreement, not merely routine paperwork after unconditional approval.
rationales.Permission to implement the merger immed: The sentence does not authorize implementation before the funding condition is met.

findings: Original more-transparent-procedure item was elementary indefinite counting.
audit.microSkill: Article-free in principle as qualified assent
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a fixed article pattern with the limits of a commitment.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting qualified approval and remaining conditions requires C1 precision.
audit.similarityNote: A commitment-limiting phrase rather than an abstract noun naming a field.

items.setupText: Choose the account of the definite reference.
items.taskText: "A donor offered to fund the restoration. The generosity surprised everyone, but the conditions did not." What identifies "the generosity"?
options: The quality inferred from the donor's offer in the preceding sentence
A separate charitable act mentioned before the quoted passage
The donor's general character across all previous donations
The total monetary value of every contribution to the project
items.answer: The quality inferred from the donor's offer in the preceding sentence
items.explanation: A noun need not have appeared literally before for definite reference to work. The offer makes a quality of generosity available for reference. The passage does not establish the donor's entire history or the project's total funding.

rationales.The quality inferred from the donor's of: The reader derives the quality from the event and can then identify it with the.
rationales.A separate charitable act mentioned befo: The immediately preceding offer supplies the needed connection; no separate act is required.
rationales.The donor's general character across all: The passage supports a quality displayed in this offer, not a general biography of the donor.
rationales.The total monetary value of every contri: Generosity names an evaluated quality here, not the sum of all contributions.

findings: Original Evidence sentence provided only elementary uncountable reference.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference to a quality inferred from an event
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends reference tracking beyond literal noun repetition.
audit.levelReason: The reader must infer a nominal referent from a proposition in connected prose.
audit.similarityNote: An inferred quality, unlike an associated physical part or scheduled time.

items.setupText: Choose the meaning of the article change.
items.taskText: "The laboratory performs analysis; this particular procedure is an analysis of trace metals." What does "an analysis" present?
options: One particular type or instance of an analytical procedure
Analytical work in general, without presenting an individual procedure
The specific analysis already identified by the first use of the noun
A laboratory classified by the kind of analytical service it provides
items.answer: One particular type or instance of an analytical procedure
items.explanation: Article-free analysis can name the general activity. "An analysis of trace metals" presents one analytical procedure or instance. The indefinite article does not certify validity or mark prior familiarity.

rationales.One particular type or instance of an an: The indefinite article packages the activity as an individual procedure of the specified kind.
rationales.Analytical work in general, without pres: That describes the article-free activity reading in the first clause, not the counted use an analysis of trace metals.
rationales.The specific analysis already identified: The first clause names analysis as an activity; it does not identify an individual procedure for a definite phrase to refer back to.
rationales.A laboratory classified by the kind of a: The second clause classifies the procedure, not the laboratory. Its subject is this particular procedure.

findings: Original analysis-of-records cloze tested an without teaching countable versus activity readings.
audit.microSkill: Analysis as activity versus a bounded analytical procedure
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains an article choice common in technical prose without equating it with scientific merit.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting an abstract process as an individual procedure is suitable C1 nominal precision.
audit.similarityNote: Procedural individuation, distinct from field-to-policy reference.

items.setupText: Alex once avoided crowds; now he hosts huge parties. An old friend comments on the change.
items.taskText: 'This is not the Alex I remember from university.' What does 'the Alex I remember' identify?
options: Another university friend who happened to have the same name
Alex as the person with his former habits and character
Alex as the only person in his university class with that name
Alex as a representative of everyone the speaker knew at university
items.answer: Alex as the person with his former habits and character
items.explanation: The article and following clause select Alex as remembered by the speaker. A personal name can take the when the phrase identifies a particular version, aspect, or namesake; this context favours a remembered version.

rationales.Another university friend who happened t: The context explicitly concerns a change in Alex's behaviour, not confusion between two people named Alex.
rationales.Alex as the person with his former habit: The article and relative clause select the version of Alex preserved in the speaker's memory.
rationales.Alex as the only person in his universit: The definite phrase identifies a remembered version of him; it supplies no information about classmates' names.
rationales.Alex as a representative of everyone the: The clause identifies the speaker's memory of this individual. It does not make Alex a type representing an entire group.

findings: Original only-analysis item forced the in a repeated frame.
audit.microSkill: The with a modified personal name referring to a remembered aspect
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a familiar exception to bare personal names through reference.
audit.levelReason: The learner distinguishes literal namesake reference from a contextually favoured aspect reading.
audit.similarityNote: Personal memory rather than an artwork or public portrayal.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article pattern.
items.taskText: "They elected her chair, but she continued to work as a researcher." Why is the first role bare while the second has "a"?
options: The first names an office conferred; the second classifies her continuing professional work
The first is bare because her identity is known; the second is indefinite because her identity is unknown
The first role is uniquely held, so bare chair would also be required after interviewed
The second article counts a separate research project rather than classifying the person
items.answer: The first names an office conferred; the second classifies her continuing professional work
items.explanation: After elect, a role complement can be bare: "elected her chair". "As a researcher" classifies her continuing professional activity. The article patterns do not establish pay or permanence.

rationales.The first names an office conferred; the: Elect licenses the bare role complement, while as a researcher gives an indefinite professional classification.
rationales.The first is bare because her identity i: The same known person is described in both clauses. The difference is in construction and role, not knowledge of her identity.
rationales.The first role is uniquely held, so bare: Interviewed does not license the same role complement: "They interviewed the chair" normally needs a determiner.
rationales.The second article counts a separate res: The noun researcher denotes a person, so the article classifies her professional role rather than counting projects.

findings: Original language-acquisition item was a basic article-free field name.
audit.microSkill: Bare elected office contrasted with indefinite professional classification
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents applying article omission for offices to all profession descriptions.
audit.levelReason: Coordinating two role constructions and distinguishing their functions suits C1 grammar.
audit.similarityNote: Contrasting constructions within one person's career, not simply an isolated appointment.

items.setupText: Choose the implication of the introductory phrase.
items.taskText: "A certain Mr Bell has been asking to see you." What does "a certain Mr Bell" most naturally do?
options: Introduces a named visitor without assuming shared familiarity with him
Identifies a visitor the listener is expected to recognise as the only relevant Bell
Presents Bell as an example of a familiar personality type rather than an individual
Expresses uncertainty about the surname while affirming familiarity with the person
items.answer: Introduces a named visitor without assuming shared familiarity with him
items.explanation: "A certain" can introduce a person by name while leaving their identity or relevance unsettled for the listener. Certain here does not simply mean confident or reliable.

rationales.Introduces a named visitor without assum: A certain introduces the named individual without treating identification by the listener as settled.
rationales.Identifies a visitor the listener is exp: The indefinite introduction does not assume that shared identification.
rationales.Presents Bell as an example of a familia: The visitor is an actual person asking for a meeting, not a type defined by the name Bell.
rationales.Expresses uncertainty about the surname: The construction does not itself cast doubt on the name; it marks how the individual is being introduced.

findings: Original exception-for-staff item tested only an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: A certain introducing a named but not mutually identified person
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects an unusual proper-name article pattern with assumptions about the listener's knowledge.
audit.levelReason: The conventional pragmatic effect of a certain is an advanced reference distinction.
audit.similarityNote: Listener familiarity at first introduction, distinct from remembered versions of a known person.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct version in formal prose.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: Rarely have we encountered so a compelling argument.
Rarely have we encountered such compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered so compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered a so compelling argument.
items.answer: Rarely have we encountered so compelling an argument.
items.explanation: In the formal pattern "so + adjective + a/an + singular noun", the adjective precedes the article: "so compelling an argument". The article still matches the sound of argument.

rationales.Rarely have we encountered so a compelli: The so-pattern places the adjective before the article: "so compelling an argument".
rationales.Rarely have we encountered such compelli: With such, the normal order is "such a compelling argument"; this mixes the such and so patterns.
rationales.Rarely have we encountered so compelling: This correctly uses the formal so-adjective-article-noun sequence.
rationales.Rarely have we encountered a so compelli: The degree word so cannot occupy this position after the article in the standard construction.

findings: Original only argument that was an unnatural forced-the construction.
audit.microSkill: Article position in so plus adjective plus singular noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts two similar degree constructions and preserves sound-based article choice.
audit.levelReason: The marked noun-phrase order is appropriate to C1 formal writing.
audit.similarityNote: Only so-adjective article inversion in the set.

items.setupText: Choose the grammatically correct version of the formal expression.
items.taskText: Which sentence is correct?
options: Many a promising scheme has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising schemes has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising scheme have failed for lack of maintenance.
A many promising schemes have failed for lack of maintenance.
items.answer: Many a promising scheme has failed for lack of maintenance.
items.explanation: Many a has a plural meaning but uses a singular count noun and singular verb: 'Many a scheme has failed.' Keep this formal construction distinct from ordinary 'many schemes have failed'.

rationales.Many a promising scheme has failed for l: The formal quantity expression combines the singular scheme with has even though it refers to many cases.
rationales.Many a promising schemes has failed for: After many a, use the singular noun scheme. The plural meaning does not license schemes in this pattern.
rationales.Many a promising scheme have failed for: The head noun scheme is grammatically singular in this construction, so its verb is has.
rationales.A many promising schemes have failed for: This mixes two patterns. Use either 'many promising schemes have' or 'many a promising scheme has'; a cannot simply precede many here.

findings: Original framework-for-comparing item only tested a before a consonant.
audit.microSkill: Many a with singular noun and agreement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes semantic plurality from the syntax of a formal quantity expression.
audit.levelReason: The marked many a construction and its agreement demand suit C1.
audit.similarityNote: Singular syntax with plural meaning, distinct from a good many.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation that follows from the definite phrase.
items.taskText: 'We are still searching for a framework. The framework must accommodate exceptions without treating them as errors.' How should the second sentence be understood?
options: It describes a framework already selected, while leaving open whether the framework can meet the requirement
It sets a requirement for the framework being sought, without asserting that one has been found
It refers to an earlier unsuccessful framework and describes the feature that the new one should replace
It announces that the search has ended but that the chosen framework still needs to be tested
items.answer: It sets a requirement for the framework being sought, without asserting that one has been found
items.explanation: The definite phrase can continue reference to the object of a search. It specifies what the sought framework must be like, without cancelling "still searching" or asserting that one has been found.

rationales.It describes a framework already selecte: Still searching rules out treating the definite article as an announcement of selection. The phrase continues reference to what is being sought.
rationales.It sets a requirement for the framework: Must states the desired property of the sought object. Definite reference can remain within that projected situation.
rationales.It refers to an earlier unsuccessful fra: No earlier failed framework is established. The natural link is back to a framework in the ongoing search.
rationales.It announces that the search has ended b: Changing a to the maintains reference; it does not cancel the statement that the search is continuing.

findings: Original only-framework item mechanically forced a definite article.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference to a sought object without asserting successful discovery
audit.pedagogicalValue: Counters an overstrong existence inference from the.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting reference within a search and requirement context is appropriate C1 precision.
audit.similarityNote: A desired object of search, rather than a conditional flaw or expected persona.

items.setupText: Choose the account of the fixed phrase.
items.taskText: "The reform was introduced in the hope that smaller classes would improve participation." Why is "the hope" natural here?
options: The following clause specifies the content of the motivating hope
Hope is countable only when the outcome is guaranteed
Any noun immediately before that must take the
The article proves that all participants shared the same expectation
items.answer: The following clause specifies the content of the motivating hope
items.explanation: "In the hope that" presents a motivating hope and supplies its content in the following clause. It does not promise success or establish that everyone shared the hope.

rationales.The following clause specifies the conte: This explains the content-linked definite phrase in the established expression.
rationales.Hope is countable only when the outcome: Having a hope does not guarantee its fulfilment, and countability is not determined by success.
rationales.Any noun immediately before that must ta: Compare "a claim that surprised us". A following that-clause does not impose the article mechanically.
rationales.The article proves that all participants: The phrase states the motivation for the reform, not a unanimous belief among participants.

findings: Original education-policy item allowed both general and identified policy readings.
audit.microSkill: The with the content clause in in the hope that
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches a formal purpose expression while limiting inferences about certainty and agreement.
audit.levelReason: Distinguishing motivation, content, and outcome is useful C1 reading and writing.
audit.similarityNote: Content-specified motivation, distinct from source-specified evidence.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite ordinal phrase.
items.taskText: "The diagnosis was unclear, so she sought a second opinion." Why is "a" possible before "second"?
options: It selects the second opinion from a numbered set already identifiable to the listener
It introduces an additional opinion rather than identifying an established numbered opinion
It introduces another clinician rather than another opinion, regardless of who gives it
It presents the first diagnosis as mistaken and therefore in need of replacement
items.answer: It introduces an additional opinion rather than identifying an established numbered opinion
items.explanation: Ordinals do not always require the. "A second opinion" introduces another opinion as an additional instance. "The second opinion" would identify an opinion in an established ordered set.

rationales.It selects the second opinion from a num: That would fit the second opinion in an established sequence. A second opinion introduces an additional instance without requiring such a known set.
rationales.It introduces an additional opinion rath: The indefinite ordinal phrase has the additional-instance reading: another opinion beyond the one already obtained.
rationales.It introduces another clinician rather t: The counted noun is opinion. The phrase does not itself identify or count clinicians.
rationales.It presents the first diagnosis as mista: Seeking an additional view does not establish that the original diagnosis is wrong; it may confirm or clarify it.

findings: Original more-precise-definition item only tested elementary a.
audit.microSkill: A with an ordinal meaning an additional instance
audit.pedagogicalValue: Replaces the shortcut ordinal equals the with a reference-based distinction.
audit.levelReason: The learner must distinguish an additional instance from a definite position in a known series.
audit.similarityNote: Only indefinite ordinal construction.

items.setupText: A museum editor is distinguishing statements about an extinct species from statements about its individual members.
items.taskText: The editor changes 'A dodo is extinct' to 'The dodo is extinct' but leaves 'A dodo laid eggs' unchanged. Why is the article changed only in the first example?
options: Present-tense general statements require the, whereas past-tense general statements require a
Extinction concerns the species as a whole; egg-laying can describe a representative member
The first statement names a previously identified specimen; the second introduces another specimen
The identifies the only extinct species, while a identifies one of several egg-laying species
items.answer: Extinction concerns the species as a whole; egg-laying can describe a representative member
items.explanation: A generic indefinite singular can describe a typical member, as in a dodo laid eggs. In its literal biological sense, extinct applies to a species, not an individual bird that dies. The definite singular can name that kind: the dodo is extinct. The distinction is not a tense rule.

rationales.Present-tense general statements require: Article choice is not determined by tense: a dodo has a beak is a possible generic statement, while the dodo became extinct names the species in the past tense.
rationales.Extinction concerns the species as a who: The article needs to fit the kind of property being predicated: extinction of a species versus a characteristic of its members.
rationales.The first statement names a previously i: The museum editor is making general statements, and no individual specimens have been introduced. Extinct does not literally mean that one specimen has died.
rationales.The identifies the only extinct species,: The definite article names this species as a kind; it does not claim that no other species is extinct. The indefinite example represents a typical dodo.

findings: The original collective-adjective item had weak feedback; the first replacement repeated the B2 electric-car generic-reference frame without adding a distinct learning demand.
audit.microSkill: Matching generic article reference to kind-level versus member-level predicates
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains why a generic indefinite works with some properties but not a literal species-level predicate.
audit.levelReason: Requires comparing two legitimate kinds of generalisation and rejecting a tempting mechanical tense-based account.
audit.similarityNote: An editing contrast between predicates, not another single-sentence identification of a generic class.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the fronted expression.
items.taskText: "For a beginner, the restoration work is remarkably assured." What does "a beginner" contribute?
options: An identified novice whose name the reader already knows
A comparison standard based on membership of the beginner category
A claim that exactly one beginner contributed to the restoration
A claim that the restorer has never attempted any related task
items.answer: A comparison standard based on membership of the beginner category
items.explanation: "For a beginner" frames the evaluation against expectations for someone in that category. The indefinite article classifies; it does not count all contributors or establish the restorer's complete history.

rationales.An identified novice whose name the read: The phrase supplies a category-based standard, not a name or definite identity.
rationales.A comparison standard based on membershi: This explains how the indefinite phrase qualifies the evaluation of the work.
rationales.A claim that exactly one beginner contri: The article does not state the size or composition of the restoration team.
rationales.A claim that the restorer has never atte: Beginner status does not imply zero related experience.

findings: Original only-interpretation item repeated a forced-the pattern.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite category membership setting an evaluative standard
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how a noun phrase can frame an assessment without identifying an individual.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting an implicit comparison standard suits C1 evaluative writing.
audit.similarityNote: Category-based expectations rather than professional pre-eminence or role appointment.

items.setupText: Choose the account of the contrast.
items.taskText: "We need research, not a research proposal." What distinction does the article support?
options: An activity or body of investigation versus one document proposing it
An informal conversation versus a published scientific result
A completed investigation versus a document that has already been rejected
Several studies versus several proposals
items.answer: An activity or body of investigation versus one document proposing it
items.explanation: Research is uncountable in the first phrase. In the second, the head noun is countable "proposal", so "a" introduces one document; research modifies the kind of proposal.

rationales.An activity or body of investigation ver: This identifies the head noun and reference type of each phrase.
rationales.An informal conversation versus a publis: The article contrast does not establish informality or publication.
rationales.A completed investigation versus a docum: Research need not be complete, and the proposal's rejection is not stated.
rationales.Several studies versus several proposals: The second phrase is explicitly singular; the first does not supply a count.

findings: Original interview-data sentence was a general mass-noun cloze.
audit.microSkill: Article determined by the head noun in a compound noun phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains why a research proposal is grammatical although a research normally is not.
audit.levelReason: Identifying the head of an academic noun phrase supports C1 editing accuracy.
audit.similarityNote: A compound's countable head, distinct from recategorising the same noun.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the negative article phrase.
items.taskText: "Not a word of her account was corroborated by the recordings." What does "not a word" convey?
options: One particular word lacked support, while the rest was corroborated
No part of her account received corroboration from those recordings
Her account was conclusively disproved by the recordings
The recordings contained no speech from any participant
items.answer: No part of her account received corroboration from those recordings
items.explanation: "Not a word" is emphatic: even the smallest part of the account received no corroboration from the specified source. Lack of corroboration is not itself proof that the account is false.

rationales.One particular word lacked support, whil: The emphatic phrase denies support throughout the account; it does not isolate one unsupported word.
rationales.No part of her account received corrobor: This preserves both the force of not a and the limited claim about support from the recordings.
rationales.Her account was conclusively disproved b: Not being corroborated is weaker than being disproved. The sentence does not assert conclusive falsification.
rationales.The recordings contained no speech from: The sentence concerns whether the recordings support the account, not whether they contain speech.

findings: Original an estimate item supplied only a basic unmodified sound decision.
audit.microSkill: Emphatic not a minimiser under negation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes zero support from one exception and from positive disproof.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting emphatic negative scope while preserving an evidential limit requires advanced precision.
audit.similarityNote: The only negative minimiser construction in the C1 set.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the article phrase.
items.taskText: "The explanation has a clarity that the earlier draft lacked." What does "a clarity" do?
options: Presents the current explanation as one of several equally clear versions
Presents a particular quality or degree of clearness characterised by the following clause
Introduces a separate clear passage that can be counted within the explanation
Identifies the same quality of clearness as one already established in the earlier draft
items.answer: Presents a particular quality or degree of clearness characterised by the following clause
items.explanation: Clarity is usually uncountable, but the phrase presents a characterised manifestation of that quality. The following clause contrasts the present text with the earlier draft.

rationales.Presents the current explanation as one: A modifies clarity, not explanation. It characterises the present text's quality without establishing a set of equally clear versions.
rationales.Presents a particular quality or degree: The article presents an instance of the abstract quality, and the clause distinguishes it from what the earlier text lacked.
rationales.Introduces a separate clear passage that: The bounded use concerns a quality of the explanation, not a newly introduced passage or section.
rationales.Identifies the same quality of clearness: The earlier draft is said to lack this clarity. The indefinite phrase presents the current quality rather than referring back to one already established there.

findings: Original explanation-for-non-specialists item only tested an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite article with a characterised abstract quality
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains a controlled abstract-noun use common in evaluative prose.
audit.levelReason: The learner interprets rhetorical individuation of a quality rather than merely choosing from spelling.
audit.similarityNote: Textual clarity rather than emotion, knowledge, or a countable document.

items.setupText: Amira does not practise as an architect, but she sometimes designs useful spaces.
items.taskText: A critic dismisses her by saying, 'She is no architect.' Choose the revision that states only her occupational status, without judging the quality of her designs.
options: She is not much of an architect.
She is not the architect.
She is not an architect.
She is no great architect.
items.answer: She is not an architect.
items.explanation: Not an architect neutrally denies membership of the professional category. In the critic's dismissive use, no architect suggests that she lacks an architect's competence. The revision removes that evaluation without introducing a particular architect's identity.

Not much of evaluates how good she is at the role; it retains the criticism the revision is meant to remove.
The points to a particular architect relevant to a project or conversation. Denying that identity does not deny being an architect professionally.
The indefinite noun phrase names the professional category; ordinary negation denies that category membership without rating her design skill.
This denies distinction or excellence, not professional status. It can describe someone who is an architect but not a great one.

findings: The original only-methodology frame was repetitive; the first revision repeated a degree-word-order task and depended on a potentially marginal comparative alternative.
audit.microSkill: Neutral not a classification versus evaluative no and identifying not the
audit.pedagogicalValue: Helps writers remove an unintended put-down while keeping an accurate statement of professional status.
audit.levelReason: Requires distinguishing grammatical paraphrases by evaluative force and reference rather than basic article form.
audit.similarityNote: An interpersonal editing decision about negative classification, distinct from degree-word order and countability.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation licensed by the articles.
items.taskText: "Whenever a committee appoints a chair, the chair receives a casting vote." What does "the chair" refer to?
options: The same person appointed to chair every committee
Whoever chairs a committee, whether appointed or acting temporarily
The particular appointee in each appointment covered by the rule
A chair already holding office before the appointment
items.answer: The particular appointee in each appointment covered by the rule
items.explanation: "A chair" introduces an appointee inside each situation described by "whenever". "The chair" refers back within that situation; it need not identify one person across all committees.

rationales.The same person appointed to chair every: The definite phrase is interpreted separately for each appointment. It does not require a single chair shared by all committees.
rationales.Whoever chairs a committee, whether appo: The sentence establishes its referent through the appointment just mentioned. It does not extend the rule explicitly to acting chairs appointed in no such event.
rationales.The particular appointee in each appoint: This preserves the local link from "a chair" to "the chair" under "whenever".
rationales.A chair already holding office before th: The antecedent is the appointee introduced by "appoints a chair", not a previously established officeholder.

findings: Original role-of-timing cloze offered elementary article selection and generic feedback at C2.
audit.microSkill: Definite reference dependent on a quantified situation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that the can identify a different referent on each application of a rule.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting reference under whenever requires control beyond a simple first/later-mention rule.
audit.similarityNote: Only item with a definite referent varying across quantified situations.

items.setupText: Choose the account of the article change.
items.taskText: An editor changes "There is little room for doubt" to "There is little room for a doubt of that kind". What does the added article do?
options: It presents a reservation as one bounded possibility of the specified kind
It asserts that a particular reservation is already held, despite the limiting phrase
It identifies a previously discussed reservation rather than introducing a kind
It turns all remaining uncertainty into one objection that the writer accepts
items.answer: It presents a reservation as one bounded possibility of the specified kind
items.explanation: Without an article, "doubt" names uncertainty as a general state. "A doubt of that kind" packages a reservation as an individual possibility. The negative scope of "little room" still limits it.

rationales.It presents a reservation as one bounded: The indefinite article individuates doubt while the surrounding phrase still limits room for such a reservation.
rationales.It asserts that a particular reservation: An indefinite within "little room for" does not by itself assert an existing, held reservation.
rationales.It identifies a previously discussed res: That would be the identifying function more naturally expressed by "the doubt"; the indefinite phrase characterises a possible instance.
rationales.It turns all remaining uncertainty into: The writer does not assert acceptance of an objection or equate it with all uncertainty.

findings: Original empirical-account item tested only an before a vowel.
audit.microSkill: Individuating an abstract mass noun under a limiting expression
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects countable reinterpretation with what a sentence does and does not assert.
audit.levelReason: Requires subtle interpretation of an abstract noun and the scope of a limiting phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Focuses on abstract uncertainty, distinct from emotional and material reinterpretations.

items.setupText: Choose the account of the two article functions.
items.taskText: "As the curator of the collection, she approached the purchase with the caution of a curator rather than the enthusiasm of a collector." How do "the curator" and "a curator" function?
options: Both identify her personally; the article change merely avoids repeating an identical noun phrase
The first identifies her role; the second characterises caution by a professional type
The first establishes her occupation; the second leaves whether she is a curator unresolved
The first identifies her position; the second attributes her caution to another curator's influence
items.answer: The first identifies her role; the second characterises caution by a professional type
items.explanation: "The curator of the collection" identifies her as the holder of the relevant role. "The caution of a curator" classifies the quality of her approach by reference to a professional type. It does not introduce another curator.

rationales.Both identify her personally; the articl: The second phrase invokes qualities associated with a professional category; it is not simply another identifying reference to her.
rationales.The first identifies her role; the secon: The definite role identifies her; the indefinite professional type characterises the caution she displays.
rationales.The first establishes her occupation; th: The first phrase has already established her role. Using a professional type to describe her manner does not withdraw that information.
rationales.The first identifies her position; the s: 'Of a curator' describes the kind of caution; it does not assert that an adviser influenced her.

findings: Original narrower-definition item was elementary singular counting in formal vocabulary.
audit.microSkill: Identifying role versus classifying professional quality
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates definite role identification from an indefinite professional characterisation without inventing another participant.
audit.levelReason: The decision coordinates two reference functions and a count/mass distinction in one sentence.
audit.similarityNote: Professional characterisation rather than the appointment rule used elsewhere.

items.setupText: Choose the most precise explanation of the contrast.
items.taskText: Compare "She studies education in coastal communities" with "She studies the education of the three siblings". Why does the second noun phrase use "the"?
options: A postmodifier makes education definite whenever it narrows the range of people being studied
The second identifies the siblings' educational history, while the first can retain a general reading
The second points back to an education mentioned earlier, which the first sentence must introduce
The first refers to education generally, whereas the second must refer to one course shared by the siblings
items.answer: The second identifies the siblings' educational history, while the first can retain a general reading
items.explanation: The second sentence treats the siblings' education as an identifiable object of study. Postmodification alone does not force "the": "education in coastal communities" remains general in the first sentence.

rationales.A postmodifier makes education definite: The coastal-community modifier also narrows the subject without requiring the. Restricted subject matter is not the same as an identifiable referent.
rationales.The second identifies the siblings' educ: The siblings' education can be identified through its relation to them. The other sentence treats education as a general subject within a setting.
rationales.The second points back to an education m: These are separate examples. An of-phrase can make a referent identifiable without an earlier mention of it.
rationales.The first refers to education generally,: An identifiable education can cover different schools and many experiences. Definiteness does not turn it into a single course.

findings: Original Causation item had a capitalisation cue and no advanced article contrast.
audit.microSkill: Definiteness determined by reference rather than postmodification alone
audit.pedagogicalValue: Corrects the misleading rule that an of-phrase automatically requires the.
audit.levelReason: Requires comparing interpretations and rejecting a tempting overgeneralisation about modified abstract nouns.
audit.similarityNote: Pairs field/process reference with individuated educational history.

items.setupText: Choose the interpretation of the highlighted article use.
items.taskText: "A new biography promises to reveal a Shakespeare unfamiliar to readers of the school anthologies." What does "a Shakespeare" most naturally mean?
options: A biography whose title is Shakespeare
A writer merely similar in ability to Shakespeare
An aspect or representation of Shakespeare that readers may not know
An unidentified person whose surname happens to be Shakespeare
items.answer: An aspect or representation of Shakespeare that readers may not know
items.explanation: The indefinite article allows a proper name to present one version or aspect of the known person. The biography and the reference to school anthologies support this reading of "a Shakespeare".

rationales.A biography whose title is Shakespeare: The biography promises to reveal Shakespeare; the phrase is not naming the book itself.
rationales.A writer merely similar in ability to Sh: "A Shakespeare" can mean a comparable genius elsewhere, but a biography revealing its subject favours a new view of the original person.
rationales.An aspect or representation of Shakespea: The article frames a particular portrayal of the familiar historical person.
rationales.An unidentified person whose surname hap: That reading is grammatically possible elsewhere, but the biography and anthology context identify the established writer.

findings: Original only-precedent sentence forced an elementary the answer through only.
audit.microSkill: Indefinite article giving an aspectual reading to a proper name
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows why proper names can take a without introducing a different person.
audit.levelReason: Discriminates among several legitimate meanings of a proper-name construction using discourse context.
audit.similarityNote: A biographical aspect of a person differs from the artwork-name metonymy elsewhere.
